I wanted to give this plain front yard a premium upgrade, so I grabbed my tools and got to work! Watching the real progress unfold in this timelapse is incredibly satisfying. Here is a step-by-step breakdown of how I built this modern rock garden: 1️⃣ First, I mapped out a smooth, curved border on the grass using white spray paint. 2️⃣ Next, I dug out the edge along the line and laid down a heavy-duty black weed barrier. 3️⃣ I installed a sleek stone border, block by block, to keep everything neat and contained. 4️⃣ Then came the best part—pouring and leveling tons of crisp white river rocks for that beautiful, high-contrast look. 5️⃣ Finally, I styled the space by placing a dark statement sphere, planting some architectural agaves, and adding solar pathway lights. Seeing the before and after of this build progress makes all the hard work totally worth it! 21 hours in 90 seconds👨🏽‍🌾 ⚠️Flash Warning⚠️ This house was bought near the end of 2025 and the garden was a right state!  I was called in to replace the fence panels and totally rip out the garden  (not the posts, they are a bit crooked but they are still standing😅)  I started with the fence panels, then began to totally clear the area of weeds and any other debris in the garden.  We added 2 railway sleepers at the back for a little flower bed. Then a thick layer of top soil was spread and we rolled out the turf. Then we moved 4 tonnes of hardcore to the back through the house!  Backbreaking stuff.  Thanks to my pal @Wagwarn Abel for jumping on and giving me a hand 🙏 This is obviously unfinished but I think the owner was going to slab the rest himself, so our job is done here for now! As always I wanna know what would YOU do now? There's a bed at the back that's totally empty!  I read and appreciate any comments and genuinely like reading your suggestions🙏 Thanks so much for watching anyway, follow if you haven't already for more vids like this!! Love, Tom Butler  #satisfying #timelapse #landscaping #gardening

*edit* makeover 💀  Landscape Edging ($35): I bought this on Amazon - it is a bit flimsy, but since it’s almost completely supported on either side by pavers or topsoil, it works perfectly for what I needed, which is a clean line between the pathway and the flowerbed. LMK if you want the link!  Flagstone ($270): this is mountain flagstone from Costco, but I bought them on Facebook marketplace for $100 cheaper than Costco sells them. The seller had only used like 4 pavers & didn’t need the rest - always check marketplace!! I did take some pavers from our patio that I didn’t need for this approximately 100ish sf pathway, but since we already paid for those girl math says they’re free so 🤣 Topsoil ($85): a yard of bulk topsoil for $50, once I ran out, I spent $35 on bagged topsoil. Buying in bulk >> Plants ($600 ish): This was hard to estimate because a lot of the time, I was buying plants for other parts of the house too, but it was around $600. I definitely busted the budget on this one.. lol worth it 🤠 a way to save $$$ here would have been to buy what they call nursery plants (the same plant just smaller and cheaper). If you want a list of the plants, I made a reel on that - about 10 posts back!  Mulch ($28): less than $4 a bag at @homedepot so no need to buy in bulk when it’s that cheap! Ground Cover ($90): I separated this out from the plants because this is just what I spent on the ground cover I put in the pathway. I used blue star creeper and creeping thyme! Total cost: approximately $1,108 The fence was “free” because it was all leftover material from the new fence we built on the other side of our yard 🙂 I didn’t include the shed in here cause it was pretty minimal - the cedar trim, paint and the new light altogether cost under $100 🫶🏼 • • #diy #makeover #garden  #landscape #gardening #landscaping #plants #flowers #homeimprovement #homeimprovement

Ornamental grasses do particularly well in the Northeast because many varieties are naturally adapted to cold winters, seasonal changes, and a wide range of soil conditions. Their deep, extensive root systems help them tolerate periods of summer heat and drought once established, while their dormant crowns allow them to survive freezing temperatures and return reliably each spring. Many grasses also thrive in the Northeast’s full sun and well-drained soils and require relatively little maintenance compared with many flowering plants. Their ability to handle both the cold winters and humid summers makes them a dependable choice for Northeast landscapes, while their movement, texture, and winter interest add structure to the landscape year-round.#Westchester#westchestercounty #planting #landscapedesign #Greenwich
